utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the accused be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-01-47-PT, the Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic, Alagic, and Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, I have to apologise for all inconveniences caused by the unfortunate delay at the start of this case. There were some misunderstandings evidently, but fortunately now we are all here together. As to the fact that the participants are confronted with a new Bench, I should like to introduce ourselves. Firstly, I feel obliged to give the reasons for the changes of the Bench. On the 14th of March, the Plenary of the United Nations entrusted 14 Judges, with an absolute majority, to start or continue their work as permanent Judges on the basis of a fresh mandate as from November 17th, 2001. Under this new mandate, the President confirmed, according to the Rules, the assignment of this case to Trial Chamber II. The three Judges on the Bench have been assigned the permanent Judges of Trial Chamber II. Trial Chamber II confirmed that Judge Mumba be -- or stay Pre-Trial Judge in this case. The new permanent Judges are, to my left, Judge Agius, and myself. My name is SCHOMBURG. I hope it will not be too difficult for all of you to pronounce these new names, but also to live with this newly composed Bench. Let me take the opportunity to invite all of you, although having different interests by nature, to work together in a spirit of mutual trust as a basis for good cooperation. Having said this, may I have the appearances from the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution appear Madam Jocelyne Bodson, senior trial attorney; Ms. Cynthia Fairweather, legal officer; and myself, Ekkehard Withopf, OTP trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances of the Defence. First, the ones acting on behalf of Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo, and Defence counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. I'm an attorney from Sarajevo. And together with John Jones, we are Defence counsel for General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Ibrisimovic, of Sarajevo. And together with Mr. Dixon, we represent the Defence counsel for Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As this is the first joint hearing, I would like to identify the accused as well, apologising already today for any mispronunciation of their names. Please correct me, if necessary. Mr. Hadzihasanovic, would you please raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzihasanovic, Mr. Alagic, and Mr. Kubura, this is your procedure: You are not the objects of this procedure; you are the subjects. I'll say you are always on demand and in the framework of the Rules. You have the right to address the Chamber directly. It is, of course, your right to remain silent. It is, however, my duty to inform you that, having this human right in mind, to warn you that each testimony or statement given by you can be used as evidence against you. Did you understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ALAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KUBURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And additionally, I feel obliged to inform you: On this other side, if this were a coin, not only given the case, it would come somewhere to sentencing, it is settled practice in criminal courts all over the world that any cooperation bringing us closer to the truth will militate in your individual favour. This is, of course, true too when it comes to the decision on provisional release. I may draw your attention, for example, to the decision of Mr. Krajisnik’s motion on provisional release, paragraph 21. Therefore, with the professional advice of your learned Defence counsels, you individually will have to find the avenue suiting and balancing your interests best. Turning now to the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, may I ask for your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, my name is Shabaz Dzihanovic, the Deputy Federal Justice Minister, authorised representative of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on behalf of the government of -- Bosnia-Herzegovina government to come here before the Tribunal. And I have been asked to attend this meeting, and here I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Tomislav Limov, the Deputy Internal Affairs Minister of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the authorised representative of the government of the Federation at today's court proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to emphasise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to emphasise that the Trial Chamber is extremely grateful for your appearance on very short notice and appreciates your willingness to cooperate with the ICTY on the basis of your commitments to the United Nations. We have got a lot of motions, attachments to motions, and so on. Please regard it as granted that the three Judges have read these papers very carefully and know about the contents. Therefore, I will ask you to refrain from once again bringing up these issues which have already been addressed. And the Trial Chamber today is seized only with the motions on provisional release, Rule 65; therefore, please, all parties refrain from bringing up any other additional issues. Of course the main issue is the application of Rule 65. Let us come to the core issues of this Article right now. And please be sure, both parties, that the members of this Chamber have not yet made up their minds. We're open to your submissions. In order to give some structure in the deliberations, I would like to give a kind of systematic approach and invite you to follow this: First of all, the question of the factual basis of voluntary surrender is a core issue. This was challenged by the Office of the Prosecutor. And here I want both parties to be very concrete. Is it more or less simplified extradition, or in this case, simplified surrender as we know it from international law - for example, Article 66 of the Schengen agreement - or is it additionally a voluntary arrest to that extent that it was not necessary to use any force but the persons coming on their own wish to the Detention Unit. I would like to hear some facts on this issue. Then, of course, we have to address the principle of proportionality. Of course, any procedural measure has to be proportional. A measure is in public international law proportional only when suitable, necessary, and its degree and scope stands in reasonable relationship to the envisaged target. Procedural measure shall never be capricious or excessive. If it is sufficient to use a milder measure, this measure has to be applied. This means, in concrete terms, we shouldn't touch the question whether or not detention is suitable but already attach the second step: Is it necessary that the three accused stay in The Hague, or do we really have sufficient guarantees that, first of all, they will, on order of the Tribunal, come to The Hague immediately, guarantees both from the accused and from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Here we have to go into some details. And what are the necessary or what would be the necessary measures for protecting the evidence in whole? Only in case we are not satisfied here, the proportionality, in a narrow sense, becomes a question to be answered, and there we would have to hear your submissions what would be in favour and what would be in -- contrary to the decision expected by the Defence. Therefore, I should invite parties, first of all, to stress issues of guarantees. It is in the interest of this Trial Chamber to exhaust all possible measures being less intrusive than ongoing detention in The Hague, and I invite especially the Defence counsels to give their submissions in this respect. Some issues could be, for example - I only touch more or the less 24 in seriousness of these points-what about bail bonds?What about house arrest? And with a view to avoid any danger to any evidence, how can it be granted that the accused do not have any possibility detrimental to the interests of justice, for example, by having access to official documents already or not yet identified as probative evidence in this case? In order to have a tight time schedule, we have prepared a short agenda. We'll ask the Defence counsel, if necessary, each team to self-restraint to 15 minutes each; the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 15 minutes; the Office of the Prosecutor, 30 minutes; the Defence counsel in reply, 5 minutes each; and at the -- not the end of the day but in the end of this first period, hear the accused, because without any doubt, they have the right to address the Trial Chamber themselves for approximately 10 minutes each. And I may add, of course, nobody needs to exhaust the time granted. Finally, I have to point out, also with a special view to our friends from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it is to the discretion of all participants at any point in time to request for having a hearing in closed session, but of course, closed session has to be the exception, not the rule. Therefore, the Trial Chamber invites for any carefully reasoned requests. The very last point: We have a lot of documents filed confidentially. To facilitate our work, I would say if there are no objections by the parties, the Trial Chamber will treat all motions received until now on the issue of provisional release, save attachments because they are containing matters of privacy, as no longer being confidential. Office of the Prosecutor, agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We have no objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence agrees?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's ordered that from now on, all motions received on the issue of provisional release are no longer treated as confidential ones. May we come now to the agenda as scheduled. May I ask the Defence team to start. I would say start in alphabetical order, the Defence counsel of Mr. Alagic first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with full respect for your time, I won't go into an extensive explanation of the facts which have already been set out in our motions and submissions. I shall try and be as brief as possible and put forward my views that all the conditions under Rule 65 have been fulfilled for the decision to be reached that Mr. Alagic be accorded provisional release, for him to be able to be at liberty. We have provided sufficient proof. On the other hand, I do not consider that the Prosecution has put forward a single valid reason for which the Trial Chamber would not acquiesce to our request. I shall start out from your suggestion, and let us take into consideration first the circumstances of the voluntary surrender of the accused to the Tribunal, because the Prosecution challenges the fact that it was indeed a voluntary surrender on the part of the accused. We have studied with great care all the circumstances surrounding the surrender, and in the submission and in the response by the Prosecutor to our request that a letter exists by the Deputy Prosecutor, Mr. Graham Blewitt, sent to Dr. Lagumdzija, the presiding officer of the Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina - this is to be found in annex 2 of the Prosecution response - and it stems from that that the government was not told that our clients, or rather, the accused, can surrender voluntarily. All they were given was an eight-day time limit for the arrest to be conducted. And this fact probably led the government to believe, erroneously, that it was necessary for them to be arrested. In that way, my client was left without the possibility of surrendering voluntarily, and this emanated from Rifat Culjevic's statement, which represents attachment 8 of our submission, who very clearly stated -- because he was the individual who reached General Alagic first when he was to be sent to The Hague, and it emerges from that, quite clearly, that General Alagic knew that he had to contact the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to The Hague, said he was sorry that he had not been informed a different way and thus have been able to surrender voluntarily. Furthermore, from an additional official note by the judge of the Supreme Court, Mr. Vlado Adamovic, we can see that Alagic contacted him with a written statement in which he requests that he be surrendered voluntarily. He says that he does not wish to be arrested and sent to the International Tribunal in that way. The Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted that, and he stopped extraditional arrest and sent General Alagic as somebody who was voluntarily surrendering to The Hague Tribunal. The separate question is how the arrest was conducted by the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal, and my client had absolutely no possibilities of wielding any influence on that. Let me just comment briefly the following fact, the fact that is set forward by the Prosecutor in this response. The Prosecutor says that it is understood that a voluntary arrest by a person - voluntary surrender, I'm sorry - is if there was no threat towards that person, or coercion and duress, that he would be arrested. Now, if the Prosecutor views matters in this light, then there is not a single person who has been accused by the Tribunal who would voluntarily surrender under those circumstances, because each indictment is accompanied by an arrest warrant, and if a warrant of that kind exists, and if it is -- if the person involved is told of this, then this is pressure, this is coercion, the very knowledge of that existence of that arrest warrant. I therefore do not consider that the position of the Prosecution in that respect is tenable. Without dwelling on that question any more, let me move on to the guarantees given by the government. I do not think I need read the conclusions and specific points in the government decision that we attach as addendum 14, enclosure 14 in our response to the Prosecution and the Prosecution's position. As listed, the government enumerates all the measures which it can take upon itself and issued written guarantees along those lines. The government will respect all the warrants issued by the Tribunal in order to ensure the presence of the accused and in order to adhere and fulfil all the other conditions in order to respect the decisions of this Court. I should particularly like to emphasise that the cooperation of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in this case as well, should be set aside from cooperation of all the other governments with the Tribunal in The Hague. What I want to say is that from the very inception of The Hague Tribunal, that is, since 1994, the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation, which at that time was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on the Federation, has always cooperated in full with the Tribunal. It has always shown full respect for every request made by the Tribunal, or as early on as the end of 1995 and the beginning of 1996, it arrested persons who were on its territory following orders and warrants by this Tribunal. It allowed the Prosecutor access, unhampered access, to all archives, as well as to those of the president of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there is no reason to doubt the absolute goodwill of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to act in accordance with all your orders and warrants, if they are sent. And in that respect, the government is quite different to other governments. Mr. Alagic, in addition to this, himself made a statement under oath and guaranteed that he would appear before this Tribunal, and expressed his readiness to take on and accept all the guarantees issued by the government. Let me also add that Mr. Alagic is a man of advanced age. His health has been seriously impaired; and we show this with the attachments to our submission. He has an apartment in Sanski Most, and nothing more. Even if he would like to go somewhere, he has nowhere to go. He just has his good name, the good name that he wishes to defend. And his name means something in Bosanska Krajina, and that's all he has left to him, his name and his face, and that's what he wishes to defend here in The Hague. So he is an individual whose guarantees can be found to be acceptable, and I'm sure that the Tribunal can accept them too. He has also given guarantees that he would not be a danger to witnesses or victims if he is provisionally released. All I want to say is that if my client is provisionally released, he will be living in Sanski Most, which is Bosanska Krajina, in a region of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is quite a long way off from Central Bosnia, which is where the crimes, in fact, took place. His sojourn in Bosanska Krajina cannot in any way disturb the victims or potential witnesses. His movements have briefly been restricted in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say, Mr. Alagic, in his appeals proceedings with the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with respect to another criminal offence, the result of that was that his travelling papers have been confiscated, so even if he wanted to leave the territory, he would not be able to do so. Therefore, having set out all these reasons, I consider that General Alagic, even if he wanted to, did not have the possibility of leaving the territory, and this makes his guarantee even more firm and more acceptable. Let me also make one final remark with respect to the Prosecution's stand; namely, the Prosecution, in their response to our motion for provisional release, adopted the attitude that Mr. Alagic, in view of his political position - and he was the mayor of Sanski Most - wielded great influence and could influence witnesses, and one could thereby conclude that he could come by official documents more easily, documents which could be linked to this case. All I want to say is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a little more than a year ago elections were held and that the party, whose member General Alagic was, lost the elections. That political party wields no more political influence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore this argument on the part of the Prosecution really cannot stand. Even if he did have an influence, his influence could only be limited and restricted to the region of Sanski Most, which is the area that he was the town mayor in, and the broader area of Bosanska Krajina. Let me now dwell for a brief moment on the fact that the Prosecution considers that Alagic has been accused of serious crimes, charged with serious crimes. I consider that he has not been -- or rather, the fact is that he has not been charged with genocide, the crime of genocide, or crimes against humanity. He has not been charged of ordering, aiding, or abetting a criminal offence to take place. He has been charged for omissions and failure to punish the perpetrators, which is, relatively speaking, the lowest level of responsibility in cases tried before this Tribunal. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but may I just interrupt you? Of course, we have read all the contributions on these more or less theoretical issues. May I ask a concrete question as regards the matter you mentioned before, that his passport was withdrawn? And we find this in an attachment of your motion dated the 10th of October, 2001, saying that his passport was confiscated October 1999 by the police administration of Sanski Most and based on the report from the municipal court of Sanski Most. Can you please indicate the underlying reasons for this fact that has happened in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Criminal proceedings are under way against General Alagic because of the criminal offence of abuse of official position and authority, and it was in that connection that his passport was seized from him as a guarantee that he would continue to reside in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that these proceedings are still pending? And what would you add, from your point of view, about the priority given to ICTY in these cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In such cases, yes, priority is given to the Tribunal, though the proceedings are still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. We have to go into these details and another attachment, and I'm of course grateful that you can draw our attention to this. The diplomatic passport has expired and is temporarily revoked. This has been done also in 1997 already. Can you give me additional information on the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are referring to the case that is being tried in Bosnia-Herzegovina. General Alagic, in the period, I think, between 1995 and 1996 - I'm not quite sure regarding these dates - he was the town mayor of Sanski Most. In connection with the duties he performed, an investigation was carried out and a first-instance judgement was passed, finding him guilty of abuse of official position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to go on? What is the further development in this case? Was there a sentencing, and was there an appeal?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first-instance sentence was four years of imprisonment. Then an appeal was lodged. And we expect the Appeals Chamber to be sitting shortly to consider the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be a judgement in absentia?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not as a judgement in absentia. The initial judgement was passed while General Alagic was at liberty, and our law on criminal procedure allows for the possibility of a second-instance judgement being passed in the absence of the accused and only in the presence of his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have, at this point in time, any more concrete submissions on the actual situation of your client? For example, when it comes to the question of, let's say, house arrest or bail bond, what is your view here? And can you please explain a little bit the concrete family situation of your client as of today? You've already told us he will be available at a certain address. Can you explain a little bit where this will be? Is it a house? Is it an apartment? Has he lived there for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an apartment that General Alagic has been living in for some time with his wife and his adopted son, who is a student at the Faculty of Economics in Sarajevo. He is duty-bound to make a living for his family. He was about to retire when he was extradited to The Hague Tribunal. So he would continue to live in the apartment with his family, and I think that he would accept any ruling that would imply that he had to stay in his apartment under house arrest. He doesn't have the funds to pay for any kind of bail bond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now, please, Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Like my learned friend Ms. Vidovic, I will follow the instructions you gave us regarding additional arguments to those presented in our motion for provisional release which we filed on the 16th of November and the response of Defence counsel for Hadzihasanovic to the Prosecutor's response of the 11th of December. We have also provided the Court, in addition to our response, with a large number of documents. And I will not be commenting on those documents. What I would like to begin with is to refer to your observation, Your Honour, that we need to bear in mind proportionality, that is, to see in each particular case the need for adequate measures which would guarantee to the Court the conditions under Rule 65, and that is, that would guarantee that my client, General Hadzihasanovic, would respond to any call by the Trial Chamber; and secondly, should he be provisionally released, he would not be a threat to victims, witnesses, or to any other persons. I believe that this Court, in its rulings - and also this applies, I presume, to this Trial Chamber - proceeds on the internationally recognised rights of the accused that the Statute of the Tribunal contains and which was submitted to the United Nations. Therefore, in our written motion, we have said that detention prior to trial should be exceptional and that the Court should give the opportunity to the accused to present arguments, to persuade this Court that his provisional release and liberty will not hamper the administration of justice. With respect to your first request for additional arguments, then we need to say that this first condition can be corroborated by General Hadzihasanovic's attitude towards this Tribunal and his appearance here. It is our position that General Hadzihasanovic surrendered voluntarily the moment he learnt for the first time from the competent authorities that there was an indictment issued by this Tribunal against him. The Prosecutor, as you know, has the opposite opinion. My learned friend Ms. Vidovic has described the way in which General Alagic learnt about the existence of the indictment. In the file, we find a statement by Gljiva Jasmin, an authorised official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, who on behalf of that institution was assigned the task of informing General Hadzihasanovic of a decision on extradition arrest and to hand him that same decision. From that statement issued by the person who, on the 2nd of August, 1992, wearing civilian clothes and not as a policeman, approached General Hadzihasanovic -- and you see from that statement that immediately the response of General Hadzihasanovic was that there was no need for him to be informed about it by the police, that he had always up to now responded to any call by the Tribunal, and if anyone had given him a chance of one hour or one day, he would have come to The Hague himself. This is a fact which I feel the Court should appreciate. It can also be seen from that statement that after treating those persons who conveyed to him the fact about the indictment, surrendered to extradition arrest. Therefore, this statement and other indisputable facts disprove the position of the Prosecution that General Hadzihasanovic, after being placed in extradition arrest, it was only on the 3rd of August that he expressed his will to surrender voluntarily. That will was clearly and unequivocally stated on the 2nd of August to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I must also point out, as has my colleague Ms. Vidovic, that the letter of the Deputy Prosecutor did not give the government of the Federation a chance to come to The Hague, because the government was told simply to arrest and surrender the accused, and if it fails to do so within a time period of eight days, then the SFOR would do so. Perhaps it is not quite appropriate for me to say this here in court, Your Honours, but I will say it nevertheless. The day my client appeared in court for the first time, I conveyed this fact to the Prosecutor, Madam Carla Del Ponte: It is my opinion that a State that cooperates so well with the Tribunal, as does my client, deserves to be given the chance to come alone without being escorted by any other body. I also wish to point out that the Supreme Court realised that it was a mistake and that the people wanted to come voluntarily, they were released. And in fact, they came to the airport accompanied only by their attorneys and surrendered themselves to representatives of the International Tribunal. Those are the facts. Why should the Federation government be trusted that they will carry out all instructions and that the facts are as they stand in my written motion and in my oral submissions is not something I need not repeat? I think my colleague Ms. Vidovic has already placed sufficient emphasis on that. But I think that we should have absolute trust in the guarantees provided by my client, General Hadzihasanovic, because he's a person who, ever since 1996, when many people refused to recognise the Tribunal, and never mind to cooperate with it, he cooperated on a number of occasions and gave two statements. Though he was hurt badly in a traffic accident, he responded and came to this court to testify in the Blaskic case. Then again upon the request of the Prosecution, he came to testify in the Krstic case. Therefore, a man who expressed his position towards the Tribunal in that way could not express his voluntariness in any other way but when he was told about the indictment at the front door. That is why when evaluating whether the surrender was on a voluntary basis, you should take into consideration these facts and circumstances. In assessing the value of the guarantees, I would ask you to consider all the arguments contained in our written submissions, but I also would appeal to you to bear in mind that the European Court for Human Rights, in the case Letellier against France, determined that when the only reason for continued detention is the fear that the accused will escape and avoid appearing at trial, he should be temporarily released if he's able to provide adequate guarantees. The guarantees for my client have been provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which due to all acts it has undertaken in the past and not its promises, should be trusted. My colleague Ms. Vidovic mentioned the arrest in 1996 in which I was Defence counsel. Conditions for investigations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the documentation given to this Tribunal, the subpoenaing of generals to testify here, all these are facts and arguments which are not dead letter on paper but reflect the real attitude of the government of the Federation, which guarantee that my client will also appear in court when required. There is also the guarantee of my client himself, and for the reasons already given, I think should be trusted. But his family, his wife and children, have also offered their own guarantees under oath. It is not an easy matter to send one's father and husband to trial, but they said that at any time, they would support his appearance in court. There is the question of possible additional guarantees. In the enclosures provided, we have said that General Hadzihasanovic is retired and that his pension amounts to 533 German marks. With such funds, without additional effort, he and his family can hardly survive, never mind travelling outside the borders of the country. And this also shows that he cannot provide any monetary guarantees. He has an apartment of 78 square metres in Sarajevo in which he has been residing with his family members for years. He has not left that apartment for years, nor does he intend to. I think that this also is an argument that should convince you that those guarantees are sufficient and that they confirm and speak in favour of our motion for provisional release and not to apply stricter measures towards my client than would be required for a fair treatment of any individual. Finally, you also said that we might provide some additional elements. Regarding house arrest, I can tell you that I have not discussed it with my client, but an apartment with four family members living in it is probably a place in which my client could stay, and he would not oppose it, but I don't think that would be necessary. As for the second condition, for which we have already provided arguments, that is, whether my client will wield any influence on victims and witnesses and be a danger to anyone, this Tribunal has a developed jurisdiction in this area. The suggestions of the Prosecutor that only a possibility is sufficient, that is not proper. The Court requires concrete possibilities to be established of influencing witnesses. My colleague Ms. Vidovic has already spoken about this, but let me just add that the witnesses whose statements have been taken and whose statements we have received, together with the indictment, can be divided into two groups: those who are victims and who make no mention of General Hadzihasanovic and don't know him, so I don't see how the General could have any influence over them. The others are officials in various parts of the world. He has no possibility of exerting any influence on them, and even if he did have, these are people of such integrity that they cannot be influenced. Thirdly, he lives in Sarajevo, which is quite a distance from Central Bosnia, and the position of this Court in the Brdjanin case is that even a visit to the scene of the crime cannot in itself be a reason to infer that he would be a threat to the witnesses. Finally, I wish to say that provisional release, in addition to guaranteeing the rights of my client, in accordance with international regulations, it also makes for a more adequate trial and great economies for this Tribunal. Every trip here by me and others for Status Conferences would not be necessary, and time would contribute to an expeditious and fair trial. Your Honour, I feel that all these facts presented provide a sufficient basis for you to be able to grant our request for provisional release. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just one additional question: Is there any trial pending in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My client was never convicted of any act, nor are there any proceedings against him ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I, to a certain extent, of course, agree with your view that the question of infringement of interests of victims and witnesses has to be a concrete, not an abstract one, but please let us know what can be guarantees that your client will not have access to documents, as a retired general, detrimental to the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, you have already said that my client is a retired general, and even if a general, once retired, access is difficult. Secondly, you have probably learnt from the case file that the Sarajevo collection and the entire archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina were at the disposal of the Prosecutor. Therefore, I don't see that there is any single document that my client could have without that document already being served on us to prepare for defence. Also, his word that he would not even make an attempt to get hold of any such documents, and the measures of the government, which would not allow any such access, in my view, are additional guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could it be part of a written guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client can provide additional written guarantees that we will not try to obtain access to any documents that might have a bearing on this case except those which he may review together with me in preparation of his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear answer. And another question: We know it, of course, that your client has cooperated in an, I would say, excellent way with the Office of the Prosecutor. What about his attitude in the future on the question of cooperation, taking into account that he is now in a totally different situation, having to defend himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have informed the Prosecution in writing that at this point in time, my client does not wish to make a statement to the Prosecution. How the preparation of the Defence will run, as his Defence counsel, at this point in time, I cannot say. It would be premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your contribution. May I now ask the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. As scheduled, we should go on - I beg your pardon - with Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kubura stands by the application it made for provisional release and the proposals put forward in that application. The basic question which arises at this time is whether the accused Mr. Kubura surrendered voluntarily to the Tribunal or not. According to the Prosecution, Mr. Kubura was arrested by the Bosnia-Herzegovinian authorities, and after that, in keeping with the rules and regulations, he was transported and handed over to the Tribunal. However, the Defence of Mr. Kubura cannot agree with this position as put forward by the Prosecution. All the acts undertaken by Mr. Kubura from the time he learnt that there were proceedings against him before this Tribunal indicate that he wished -- that it was his wish to surrender voluntarily in order to come before this Tribunal and be tried. It is important to mention the fact that Mr. Kubura interrupted his holiday. He was in the neighbouring state of Croatia at the time, on holiday there, and at the invitation of the BH authorities, he returned to the country forthwith. There he was told of the situation, that is to say, that there were proceedings against him at this Tribunal, and he was given a document to that effect by the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, he was placed in extraditional arrest, and the following day he made a voluntary statement saying that he was voluntarily surrendering and wished, of his own free will, to travel to The Hague. Let me mention one point in this regard. In no way was Mr. Kubura offered the possibility, either by the BH authorities or by The Hague Tribunal, of expressing freely and voluntarily his attitude with respect to surrender to the Tribunal. Namely, he was arrested according to the domicile regulations and the Criminal Code of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina which regulates -- they are Articles 62 to 69 of that code. That is to say, that when detention was prescribed according to the Law on Criminal Procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the defence -- that is to say, defence becomes obligatory for Mr. Kubura; not only for Mr. Kubura, but for each and every individual deprived of liberty. Those rights were not read out to Mr. Kubura. He was not able to have contact with attorneys of his own choice, or ex officio at all, who would indicate to him the possibility and the existence and the chance that he surrender voluntarily to this Tribunal for trial. Those elementary rights were curtailed. When he first had contacts with his attorneys and when they expressed these rights to him, Mr. Kubura said that he wished to travel to The Hague voluntarily. He confirmed that statement of his in front of the Supreme Judge of the Supreme Court of the Federation, Mr. Adamovic, and we attached that letter in our application. Therefore, the conclusion is that Mr. Kubura voluntarily demonstrated that he wanted to go to The Hague. None of his actions indicate that in any way whatsoever he was obstructing either the instructions of the BH authorities or the Office of the Prosecution. Therefore, viewing the statements attached to the application and those from the representatives of the Internal Affairs Ministry of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we can confirm and assert that it was a case of voluntary surrender and that the Prosecution's position is completely unfounded. The Prosecution pleads that he was arrested twice. If he was arrested by the BH authorities and if the proceedings were interrupted, then there was absolutely no reason for him to be arrested again by The Hague Tribunal. All that had to be done was to have given him -- set out the opportunity of him going to The Hague, and that is quite clear. I should particularly like to express one more point, and that is that any omissions on the part of the BH government, in the sense of indicating to Mr. Kubura the possibility of surrendering voluntarily, cannot make Mr. Kubura's position aggravated, because he did not have the possibility of expressing his own will. As soon as he did have this opportunity, he showed quite clearly that he wanted, without the pressure of being arrested, or any other coercion or under duress of any kind, to appear voluntarily before this Tribunal and attend the trial. Therefore, it is the position of the Defence that we propose to the Trial Chamber that as Mr. Kubura surrendered voluntarily to The Hague, this ought to be accepted, and not the viewpoint of the Prosecution as presented. As far as the measures that the government has proposed in the case that Mr. Kubura be provisionally released, the Defence is not in a situation to comment as to whether the government will stand by their promises and guarantees or not. We have the representatives of the government. But the Defence team, like Mr. Kubura himself, who signed his own statement, are of the opinion that Mr. Kubura will respect all the measures set forth by the government should he be provisionally released, as well as all the instructions of the Tribunal in that regard. I do not want to repeat what my learned colleagues Ms. Residovic and Ms. Vidovic have already said, the attitude of the Bosnian government towards this Tribunal and its cooperation from the very start. I think that the measures that have been proposed will be abided by the government, and if the government acted properly during Mr. Kubura's arrest, then there is no reason to believe that they will not stand by all the guarantees that they have issued. As far as the family situation of Mr. Kubura, you have all the documents relative to that. You can see that the situation is very precarious as far as his family is concerned. He is a father of three minor children. Their ages range from 5, 10, and 11. His wife is unemployed. He doesn't even have an apartment and has not solved his residential problems. So his detention in The Hague would make that situation even more grave and bring his family into a highly precarious situation. As to the possibility of wielding any influence on victims and witnesses, a point that has been raised in these proceedings, I agree with the attitude presented by Ms. Residovic and say that we must look at this aspect realistically. His behaviour and conduct so far when he was present in the region does not indicate that he wished to enter into contact with witnesses in any way. So until we don't have a realistic danger of this, I do not think that remarks of this kind stand. I think they are unfounded. And the Tribunal and the Prosecution has an open telephone line to all -- for all witnesses and victims in any cases tried before this Tribunal, and if any realistic danger did exist, then there are government measures and Tribunal measures that are highly effective and efficient to arrest any attempts of that kind and sanction conduct of that kind. And for every accused, as for Mr. Kubura as well, there is a trial period. So in order to assess a realistic danger, we must look at this trial period. And the accused will show by -- will show by way of his conduct what this will be. And he has already stated that he is willing to recognise all the decisions of this Tribunal and the government measures expressed in the guarantees that they issued. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Also the same question in the direction of your client. Is there any trial or any prosecution pending against your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client has never had any proceedings brought against him in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the -- these are the first proceedings against my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The actual housing situation, of course, should never be detrimental to the question of whether provisional release will be granted or not, but we should know what will be the address, in future, of your client. You pointed out in your motions that -- he can't stay any longer in the former apartment but seeks for a new one. Is this already settled?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, there is a temporary solution and a new address. And I think we mentioned that new address in the attachment, but if not, I can send it on to the Tribunal. But he has still not been able to buy up this flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And also additionally, what would be your position as regards house arrest and what would be the position that there is a certain guarantee given that your client, knowing now about the indictment, will have no improper access to documents detrimental to the interest of justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client will make a statement to the effect that he will not have access to any documents which might be harmful to the interests of justice and the conducting of this trial. He is an office of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has been suspended, and he does not have any access, not only to archives but even to go to his job should he be provisionally released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Defence. Now, I believe, really the time is ripe that I may ask the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please come here a little bit closer to us that we can hear your direct comments, acting as friends of this Tribunal. Who wants to take the floor first, please? I understand Mr. Limov.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzihanovic. Your Honours, may I, with respect to the case of Mr. Alagic and General Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Kubura, as representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina state the following, and the Deputy of the Federal Justice Minister as well: You yourselves have become convinced that the -- that cooperation between the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Tribunal in The Hague has always been exemplary and that both the governments have shown this by virtue of their conduct, both previously and in this particular case. What the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to do, and the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, everything was done without a single dilemma. We never asked ourselves whether it should be done or not. We went ahead and did it in order to enable this case to be brought to trial before The Hague Tribunal. Furthermore, upon the request of the Defence counsel of General Hadzihasanovic, Alagic, and Colonel Kubura, the government of the Federation, on the 8th of October, 2001, reached a conclusion and decision that in keeping with the principles of cooperation with The Hague Tribunal that it would respond to every invitation and request on the part of The Hague Tribunal and respond to all the demands made of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this concrete case, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina expressed its readiness to respond to the invitation from the Trial Chamber in order to make a statement before the Tribunal with respect to guarantees on respect of the conditions set by the International Tribunal for persons accused of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, and we have three accused before us. On the 6th of December, 2001, the Defence of these accused once again appealed to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina for it to issue detailed measures which the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina would undertake or which it would be ready to undertake, and they consist in the following - these measures refer to all three accused persons. At a meeting of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on the 10th of December, 2001, it was decided to undertake the following: First, the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in case of the decision to be taken for the provisional release of the persons, guarantees are issued for each of the stipulated persons. It will ensure that the representatives of the Bosnian government and the Federal Justice Ministry and Federal Internal Affairs Ministry will accompany the individual to Sarajevo if they are provisionally released, and they will ensure that they come back to the Tribunal for trial and will supply escorts to the airport and transfer these individuals to The Hague authorities, as stipulated by the Court. Second, during the sojourn of the accused on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the federal organs and cantonal organs will undertake the following measures and activities: They will ensure that during the trial or proceedings, the accused Mehmed Alagic, the accused Enver Hadzihasanovic, and the accused Amir Kubura should stay on the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and once they reach Sarajevo, that they will hand over their travel documents and passports to the international department in Sarajevo; that they will report to the local police station in their place of domicile once a week; that the Federal Ministry of the Interior, in cooperation with the Cantonal Internal Affairs Ministry in Sarajevo and in the Sanski canton and the other cantons where the accused are domiciled, in cooperation with the IPTF, undertake operative and tactical measures and activities to control the sojourn of the provisionally released accused to defend themselves while at liberty and that if any attempt be made to escape which the accused -- that the organs under point 6, the competent organs and authorities of Internal Affairs would undertake the detention of these persons. We also undertake that the named persons will be domiciled at the address they have given to the Tribunal. If there are any changes, the Tribunal will be informed thereof. We shall also undertake to guarantee that they will not contact any witnesses or victims, that we will ensure that they will not talk to the media about their indictments, and that the accused persons will respond to every instruction issued by this Tribunal. The government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina will take it upon itself to send out reports at least once a month to the Tribunal stating that the individuals are abiding by the conditions set out here. The government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina takes on the obligation of reporting to the Trial Chamber as to whether the accused have violated any of their obligations or whether they are adhering to those obligations. So much from me for the moment. I'm at your disposal for any further questions you may wish to ask me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Additional comments from the side of your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for giving me the floor. I shall add a few words to what my colleague Dzihanovic said with respect to the police, because it is clear from the measures listed that the police have special responsibilities to implement these above-mentioned measures should the Tribunal rule to provisionally release the accused. I, of course, will not repeat the measures listed, but I wish to say that upon the instructions of the Prime Minister of the Federation yesterday, I had a working meeting with Ministers of the cantons, the Sanski, Dojbojski, and Sarajevski cantons, and at that meeting we specified their obligations pursuant to the guarantees provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Should the Tribunal decide to grant provisional release for Generals Hadzihasanovic and Alagic, as well as Colonel Kubura, the Federal MUP, Ministry of the Interior, is capable of implementing all these measures as well as any other instructions from the Tribunal within the framework of its terms of reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The first point to be addressed is, of course, in case the Trial Chamber could -- would come to the solution of granting provisional release but expecting more restrictive measures and guarantees, would the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina be ready to execute orders, for example, a more restrictive approach saying they have to stay in their town, be it Sarajevo, be it another town? Or additionally, even when it would come to house arrest, would this be feasible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be feasible, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the appropriate ministries would implement any orders from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I take it as granted that you would be ready and prepared to give this in writing to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to address to the representative of the Ministry of Justice a very crucial question. We are aware of the fact that a trial is pending against one of the accused here in the ICTY. What is your position on the relationship between both pending trials, and can you tell us a little bit more about the allegations in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the proceedings in domestic courts that was referred to during the statements by Defence counsel, the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the judiciary will give priority to the proceedings in this Tribunal. As regards the specific content of the charges, I must admit that I am not informed in detail about those charges, as the Ministry of Justice, according to the principle of division of competencies, has no authority over the activities of the courts as independent bodies. But if necessary, the competent court could provide information to this Trial Chamber regarding the specifics of that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, when it comes to, possible guarantees, we have to be very precise. I take it as granted that it is also your view that it would be the responsibility of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina to enforce the orders of ICTY, and -- the ICTY, of course, is not interested in internal affairs, especially when it comes to the responsibility of cantons. In addition, there are only a very few points, but they have to be addressed. What about the costs for the transport to Bosnia-Herzegovina and back to The Hague? Is the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina ready to grant that they take these costs?

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards expenditures linked to this and other similar cases, that is a question for which we do not have a solution in the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in this specific case, should the Trial Chamber grant provisional release for these accused, then we will have to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be the time frame needed to provide the Court with an additional guarantee to this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These guarantees that you have mentioned and which may be missing with respect to certain details, we can commit ourselves to provide those comments within a few days in accordance with the Court's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I see there are no other questions right now. I thank you very much for coming here, and I would ask you, just in case there will be new questions, we would highly appreciate if you could stay until the end of this hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This hearing will be adjourned now for 20 minutes, so that will mean we start again 10 minutes to 5.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the hearing on provisional release be resumed. I was told that the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina wants to take the floor for another minute. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I would like to speak, with your permission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please repeat, because the accused hadn't been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would request, on behalf of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to be allowed to say a few more words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DZIHANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Allow me just to add by saying, in answer to your question as to the resources that would be provided to cover the costs of travel for the accused should they be provisionally released, I have had contact by telephone with the Prime Minister of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and his response was that I am free to state that the government of the Federation will provide a way of financing the travel of the accused for every hearing here at the Tribunal at any time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional clarification. Now we turn to the Office of the Prosecutor. And you know the arguments of the Defence counsel now, and the Trial Chamber really would invite you to address, first of all, the question of whether or not we can speak of voluntary arrest, and especially what you have expected the accused to do more than they have done in the concrete case; and the question, of course, of additional measures: Would they be sufficient for you to have the guarantee, from your point of view, that the accused will appear for standing trial? And the last point, of course, is: Could you please give the Trial Chamber a little bit more information on the severeness of the crime from your point of view? I want to add that it goes without saying that the arguments of the Defence stating that a case - I quote, “it's only a case of 7(3)” - has no merits because we have to look into the concrete law, and a case of 7(3) may be even more severe crime than the one under 7(1). So we shouldn't waste our time with this issue, but please, as pointed out by the Defence, also the Trial Chamber would be interested to hear something more in detail what it's about in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BODSON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have just been entrusted with this case. I give the floor, therefore, to Mr. Withopf. If necessary, I will make some additional remarks after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, following your advice, I will focus on the crucial issues only. Simultaneously, I will put forward additional information as requested, and I will also respond to issues raised by the Defence. Rule 65 details two requirements for provisional release. The Trial Chamber must be satisfied of both: that the accused will appear for trial and that the accused will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. But even if these requirements are met, that does not mean that provisional release has automatically to be granted. There is no automatism. Rule 65, accordingly, explicitly says "may be granted," "Provisional release may be granted," meaning the Trial Chamber has the discretion to refuse the order notwithstanding the applicant has established the two matters. That's an issue the Defence, for obvious reasons, did not consider too much. Therefore, I will, in particular, expand on these issues. Coming to the first and main issue, the issue whether it is ensured that the accused will appear for trial and whether it has been a voluntary surrender or whether it has been an arrest, I will cover this matter with regard to all of the accused, Hadzihasanovic, Alagic, and Kubura, together, since it's the opinion of the Prosecution that the situation with regard to all three of the accused is a very, very similar one. With regard to the voluntary surrender, I want to stress that only the situation before the accused, before all of the three accused were put in extraditional arrest is of relevance; everything that happened afterwards is not. A voluntary surrender is, per definition, excluded after an arrest. I come to the affidavits of Mr. Kljucka, Mr. Culjevic, and Mr. Faik, and I actually want to quote. The first one is the one of Gljva Jasmin, and he tells the story that he, together with two more authorised officers, served General Hadzihasanovic with the decision of the Supreme Court on extraditional arrest. We have the same situation with regard to Alagic and with regard to the accused Kubura. The first impression is as if he would have returned from the Croatian coast from his annual leave knowing that he has been indicted. But if you read the affidavit related to him, the affidavit by Lusija Faik, it becomes obvious that on the Croatian coast, he was never told that an indictment has been issued. This individual, Mr. Lusija Faik, says in his affidavit: "Amir Kubura immediately said that there was no problem, that that should have been said to him straight away so he could have taken his family, as his wife and three minor children stayed at the coast in Croatia." I think, based on this information, there's only one conclusion possible. It hasn't been a voluntary surrender. It has been - and I would call it - an arrest without resistance. With regard to Kubura, it's quite normal that he, as a serving soldier, responded to the call of his commanding officer and that he reported back. Also with regard to him, there is not a very different situation as compared to his two co-accused. The fact that all of the three accused in the course of the local Bosnian extradition proceedings waived their rights is not of any relevance. As a matter of fact, the accused were already imprisoned when they did so, and this fact is actually reflected in the official press release of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovinian government. In addition, the head of the Sarajevo field office of the ICTY, Mr. Jan van Hecke, corroborated on Thursday, the 2nd of August, 2001, that the three accused had been arrested - and I quote, the word "arrested" - at their homes at approximately 0700 hours that morning, following an operation of the Ministry of Interior. Secondly, there's a legal consideration in this regard. Rule 58 of the Rules says the obligation as laid down in the ICTY Statute prevail over any national law on extradition. The reference to the national jurisdiction made by the Defence and made by the accused is therefore not really helpful. As a consequence, the Prosecution remains and maintains its position. It hasn't been a voluntary surrender. It has been an arrest without resistance. I'm turning now to the issue of the guarantees. The Prosecutor appreciates the guarantees as provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As they were detailed today, the Prosecution considers them as also being relevant in practice and sufficient in practice. However, the Prosecution wants to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the Bosnian authorities tried to implement the national extradition proceedings contrary to Rule 58 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As a result, there are still some doubts on the value of these guarantees. The Prosecution's overall assessment with regard to the first matter as provided in Rule 65(B) is, therefore, there is no voluntary surrender and some doubts remain with respect to the guarantees provided. I am now turning to the second matter as provided in Rule 65(B), outlining that the accused will not pose a danger to any victim, to any witness, or other person. The Prosecution concedes that there are no instances of concrete intimidation related to the accused. However, the following incidents should be kept in mind: When the accused were arrested and taken to The Hague, the Bosnian authorities made public comments that they would do all they could do to help the accused. Such public statements made by senior Bosnian officials was immediately, very immediately, interpreted by the Prosecution witnesses as a threat against them. And furthermore, the accused were in command of the Mujahedin, and it is well known that there are still many of them living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly in the area of Central Bosnia. It would be no surprise if these Mujahedin would be willing to help out their former superiors. Just for illustration, I want to provide the Trial Chamber with a few instances that happened within the last years. And I want to stress again these instances are not related to the accused; however, they illustrate the situation down in Central Bosnia. On 25th August 1998, a nail bomb was placed outside the front door of Ivo Mirzo [phoen]. Jovo Mirzo [phoen] is a Prosecution witness in this case. He's an outspoken member of the Croat community in Bugojno, and he is a prominent local HDZ politician. Four or five local Muslims were eventually charged with the attack, and at least one received a substantial prison sentence. Another incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Before you go on with such examples, could you show the Trial Chamber the link between these occasions and these crimes committed and the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These illustrations that I'm about to give to the Trial Chamber should show the situation in Central Bosnia as such and what could happen. And I repeat myself: We cannot prove there is a link to the accused, and I stay away from such an allegation. However - and I will expand on this issue later on - it seems to be of quite an importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, may we ask why the Prosecution hasn't raised these very specific objections at any time in the past? We wrote to the Prosecution some time ago to inquire as to whether they had any specific objections to provisional release. Again, we filed our applications for provisional release calling on the Prosecution to let us know if they had any specific particularised allegations. We've had absolutely nothing until now about these grounds for refusing provisional release, and I think it's quite unacceptable that we should be ambushed with whatever the Prosecution is going to outline now as to threats to witnesses and whatnot of which we have been given no forewarning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber finds that the -- the Office of the Prosecutor should concentrate on those issues being -- yes, the central points of this hearing and not to confuse us with new additional elements and information where we can't see the relevance for the decision to be taken today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I appreciate your comments, and we therefore turn to different issues. With regard to the accused Alagic, I want to mention his criminal background, even if it's only the abuse of an official position, but it shows that he has some background. The Prosecution's assessment with regard to the second matter, therefore, is as follows: Although so far no incident of intimidation has been proven, there's a high potential regarding further intimidation. I'm now turning to the issues that fall within the discretion of the Trial Chamber. First of all, and that -- actually, in the context of the previous issue, the effect of a provisional release on the situation in Central Bosnia. It can be anticipated that a provisional release would have a negative impact on the relations of Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia, and such a provisional release, if granted, would have a very negative impact on the willingness of witnesses to testify. The Prosecution may face serious problems with Prosecution witnesses and potential Prosecution witnesses. For the witnesses, from their view, provisional release, if granted, would make the case look weak, and such a situation could have a serious impact on the willingness of the witnesses to testify or to give a witness statement. The third issue, with regard to proportionality. The accused so far spent only four months in custody. They were transferred to The Hague in the beginning of August. A trial date is envisaged for April 2002. Compared to other accused of the Tribunal whose trial dates were much later, the accused in the present case did not spend substantial time in prison. The Prosecution submits that similar situations should be treated equally. I'm turning to the fourth point with regard to the discretionary issues, the matter of cooperation, as it has also been stressed by the Trial Chamber. It's a matter of fact that the accused cooperated with the Tribunal as court witnesses: Hadzihasanovic and Kubura in the Blaskic case; the accused Hadzihasanovic, furthermore, in the Krstic case, and/or gave witness statements. But I need to stress that in all instances, they were heard as witnesses against their former enemies and, as such, they were obviously and apparently willing to cooperate. The accused Hadzihasanovic and accused Kubura were called as witnesses in the Blaskic case. During their testimony, they had to answer questions of the Defence with regard to some crimes that form part of the indictment against them. They either denied that crimes had happened or their knowledge about such crimes. The Prosecution considers such a cooperation as limited. Furthermore, since they have been arrested, all three of the accused exercise their right to remain silent. There is no further cooperation any more. With regard to the family hardship, the Prosecution maintains its position as laid out in the response. I do not want to be repetitive. I only want to mention that it's interesting -- it's interesting enough that the accused Hadzihasanovic has not shown that he had engaged in additional jobs before he was arrested and that the accused Kubura does not make any statement whether he still gets a salary from the Bosnian government. With regard to the health condition, in the opinion of the Prosecution, this is only a relevant factor with regard to the accused Alagic. The medical examination has been ordered. I understand that the medical examination has not yet been carried out. Therefore, the Prosecution's final position depends on the result of such a medical examination. This leads to the conclusion that the Prosecution maintains its request that the motions of Hadzihasanovic and Kubura be denied. Concerning the accused Alagic, the Prosecution's position will depend on the result of his medical examination. With regard -- or in the event that the Trial Chamber thinks about to grant provisional release, the Prosecution wants to have imposed certain conditions on the accused as follows: A guarantee that a designated official of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall take custody of the accused from the Dutch authorities at Schipol airport at a date and time to be determined by the Trial Chamber; furthermore, that they accompany the accused for the duration of their travel to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that they accompany the accused back from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Schipol airport and deliver the accused back to the Dutch authorities at a date and time to be determined by this Trial Chamber; in addition, that the local police will ensure that the accused report to the police station each day, maintain a log and file, and file a monthly written report confirming the accused's compliance, and immediately report the failure to attend by the accused to the Tribunal; in addition, detain the accused immediately should they attempt to escape or breach any of the terms of their provisional release and advise the Tribunal so that arrangements for his transfer back to the Tribunal can be made; in addition, that whilst on provision release, the accused shall remain within the confines of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; furthermore, that whilst on provision release, the accused shall surrender their passports to the International Police Task Force, IPTF, or the field Office of the Prosecutor in Sarajevo; in addition, that whilst on provisional release, the accused shall report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I will do so. Furthermore, that the accused shall report each day to the local police; in addition, that whilst on provisional release, the accused shall consent to have the IPTF check with the local police about its presence and to the making of occasional unannounced visits to the accused; in addition, that whilst on provisional release, the accused shall undertake not to have any contact whatsoever nor in any way interfere with any person who may testify at their trial; in addition, that while on provisional release, the accused indicate not to speak to the media or make any public statement; and finally, that the accused shall undertake to comply strictly with any order of this Trial Chamber varying the terms of or terminating their provisional release. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, the answer to the question whether a case is ripe for provisional release or not is a very individual one, and we have to take into account the individual situation of each human being. I appreciate very much that we learnt from the Defence counsel in a very honest approach about the problems with the passport and the trial pending in Bosnia. Could the Office of the Prosecutor please provide the Trial Chamber with her view on the relationship of this case, of this ongoing trial in Bosnia? Do you have any further information on the underlying factual basis? And in addition, what is your point of view, what is the impact on the question of provisional release given the case the trial goes on? From the point of view of the Prosecutor, can the question of non bis in idem arise? And additionally, what would be the situation if this imprisonment would be upheld and Mr. Alagic would have to serve imprisonment in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To answer the questions, first, we don't have any other concrete information on the local -- with regard to the local proceedings. However, it's obviously a case alleging that Mr. Alagic abused his power in an official position. Therefore, the Prosecution thinks that the question of non bis in idem will not arise. And with regard to the third question, the Prosecution is of the opinion that the international proceedings supersede over the national proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it as given there is no more -- any other --

utterances.speaker: MS. BODSON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No further remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We turn once again to the Defence counsel. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I shall be very brief and respond to the points made by the Prosecutor. First of all, the Prosecutor reproached the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the effect that the statements of officials were not in conformity with Rule 58, and I wish to draw attention to the fact that Rule 58 has to do with the obligations of the cooperation of states according to Article 29 of the Statute, whereby states are obliged to cooperate with the International Tribunal. The Prosecutor and all of us know that the Tribunal consists of Trial Chambers, the Prosecution and the Defence. Therefore, statements by officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina are precisely in line with the behaviour required by Article 29 of the Statute, so that I think this observation cannot be accepted. I repeat that the position of the Prosecution, in spite of all the arguments given by us that the clients apparently voluntarily surrendered after they were arrested, is not in accordance with the facts, because they gave their first statements on the 2nd, prior to the arrest, and two of us three counsels came voluntarily to representatives of the International Tribunal, to whom our client surrendered without any resistance. Thank you, Your Honour, for drawing the attention of the Prosecution not to introduce into these proceedings elements and facts that are not relevant to this case. Another point I wish to make is the attempt by the Prosecution to call in question the full cooperation of my client with the Tribunal and the Prosecution. I think that it is not in accordance with the Rules and the Statute of this Tribunal, because my client -- and there is ample evidence about that, and his statements have been provided as supporting material with the indictment, are relevant to this case, and I think that the Trial Chamber cannot accept any interpretation at the expense of the accused if the accused is resorting to his rights under Article 21. Therefore, this cannot be adversely interpreted or taken as prejudicial to the client. The guarantees proposed by the Prosecution, I think, are already contained in the guarantees given by the government, and there's no dispute that my client will accept those terms.
