As for the seriousness of the charges, I would like to draw the attention of the Court to the European Court of Rights in the case ^ Jacob against Bulgaria, that the Court ruled that the seriousness of charges cannot justify extended pre-trial detention. So even if they were such charges per se, they could not be an argument that the Prosecution can rely on. Finally, in connection with the possibility of influencing witnesses and victims, I should like to draw your attention to the ruling regarding the motion for provisional release in the Brdjanin/Talic case last year, whereby the Tribunal developed its own jurisdiction and explicitly stated that the fact that the accused may be released to the area where the crimes were allegedly committed in itself does not show that he will bring pressure to bear on victims and witnesses and be a threat to them. Furthermore, the very possibility that provisional release may jeopardise the readiness of witnesses to testify does not represent a threat according to the provisions of Rule 65. Those are my additional arguments. I would just like to add, Your Honours, that we have prepared a statement, which my client is ready to sign and hand over to you today, in which he says that he is ready to carry out all the conditions ordered by the Court and is also ready to accept measures that this Trial Chamber might pass regarding restriction of movement. So would you allow my client to sign this statement so we can attach it to the other documents already filed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm speaking on behalf of General Alagic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. I'm speaking on behalf of General Alagic. I'll just make a few brief points, but of necessity, the points I'll make will be a bit longer than I had planned, given that there were a number of issues which we heard from the Prosecution which have never been raised before. So this is the first time that we've had an opportunity to respond. The first point concerning voluntary surrender, I note that the Prosecution didn't, in fact, answer the question which you posed, which was, in essence, what more could the accused have done, given the circumstances that they were arrested and they were willing to surrender at the Tribunal. In effect, the Prosecution's letter to the Bosnian authorities left no scope whatsoever for a voluntary surrender, and therefore it's a bit rich for the Prosecution to say that the accused didn't voluntarily surrender and therefore that's the reason for refusing provisional release, when their very own actions deprive the accused of that possibility. But what's also interesting is that the Prosecution raised the point that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina started to implement extradition proceedings, and it seemed that the suggestion was that this casts a doubt on whether the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be able to effectively arrest the accused and transfer them to The Hague. But in fact, what's interesting about that assertion is that, in effect, that recognises that the accused waiving any procedures which they could have raised in Bosnia to object to extradition in fact did facilitate their delivery here. They were delivered here, they were delivered here speedily, and the Prosecution in effect concedes with that statement that it was made easier by the accused. So even they, even in circumstances where the accused were deprived of the right to voluntary surrender, in fact, they did all they could, and the Prosecution must admit that actually was effective. Secondly, the Prosecution drew attention to the fact that the accused, or General Alagic, is now no longer being cooperative. But in fact, the Prosecution is wishing to interview Mr. Alagic at this stage, after he's been indicted, for the purpose of this investigation in this trial, in essence, wishing to interview him, I imagine, in order to obtain incriminating statements from him. In no system in the world would it be - at least, not in my system - would one imagine the Prosecution continuing to obtain evidence from the accused after he had already been indicted. So I submit that in the circumstances, it's really unreasonable to hold against General Alagic the fact that he's no longer cooperating, i.e., no longer admitting to be interviewed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, Counsel: Of course you're right, but isn't it true, having the right to remain silent in mind, that there can also be a cooperation or cooperative attitude of an accused in a certain case? And what is the expression or the position of your client in this concrete case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution were wishing to interview General Alagic in relation to other cases, that would be one matter. There's been no indication of that. That obviously would be one situation in which General Alagic might be in a position to aid the Prosecution without jeopardising his own privilege against self-incrimination. Secondly, there's the possibility of immunised testimony. If the Prosecution had offered to allow General Alagic to be interviewed by their office, but subject to the condition that nothing that he could -- nothing that he said would be used against him in this trial, then again that would provide scope for General Alagic continuing to cooperate with the Prosecution. Neither of those possibilities have been mooted by the Prosecutor. If they are, then we can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably you are aware that the underlying reason for my questions is, of course, that the Trial Chamber has to find out: Are there any reasons distinguishing this case from the case of Madam Plavsic? And as you know, in both cases, there was a point made: voluntary surrender, and, in addition, cooperation with the Office of the Prosecutor in the future. I never would ask your client if he doesn't want to cooperate, but I want to have your attitude, your approach to this question in this present moment of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter in relation to that which I wish to address, Your Honour, is the fact that there is a danger here that if cooperation of the accused is to become a sine qua non of the Prosecution not objecting to their provisional release, then there's very dangerous scope there for pressure to be applied to an accused to make him give statements which he perhaps is not inclined to do. There is that danger, which is a matter I was going to come to later. But the effect on witnesses in Central Bosnia has been mentioned of the provisional release. Well, that's exactly the same situation that General Sefer Halilovic is in, and in that case the Prosecution is not objecting, as far as I understand it, to his provisional release, and as we know, Sefer Halilovic is cooperating with the Tribunal, with the Prosecution. Now, as I said, that creates dangerous scope for the Prosecution, in effect, saying, "Cooperate with us or we'll ensure that you remain in custody for a long time before your trial starts." And I think the Chamber should be very astute to ensure that that sort of pressure isn't applied. If I can move on to the mention of the Mujahedin. The Prosecution began to suggest that since there are cases that the accused controlled the Mujahedin, that in effect there are hoards of Mujahedin out there who are willing to go and intimidate witnesses or interfere with evidence. Now, first of all, I would say General Alagic is presumed innocent at this point. It's not to presume that the charges which the Prosecution have laid in the indictment are irrefutably true. And in any event, the Prosecution's case is not that General Alagic ordered the Mujahedin to do anything. It's that he failed to prevent them from doing anything. So in any event, even that suggestion contradicts the Prosecution's own case in the indictment. Finally, Your Honour, I think that would be my replies to what the Prosecution said. I did want to just put into context all of what you've heard today. Obviously, the Chamber has heard a great deal of discussion on this matter, and I won't go through all the various factors again. But Your Honour referred earlier to the question of proportionality. I would submit that it is disproportionate to keep the accused in custody in circumstances where there are much less Draconian methods to ensure that the accused do appear for trial. A curfew is a possibility, an order that the accused be at his residence after a certain hour, at which point the authorities can check that he's there, and by various means, or house arrest. As indeed the Prosecution recognised towards the end of their speech, there are other methods available. Finally, I would just like to put in context the test, in essence, which you have to apply. It's long been said at this Tribunal that the Tribunal is at a disadvantage and that it doesn't have its own police force and therefore it has to rely on national authorities. And generally, where one has been dealing with Republika Srpska and initially Croatia, it is true that there were not willing authorities on the ground willing to execute warrants. In this case, I think it's abundantly clear that the Bosnian authorities are fully willing to cooperate. So in effect, one has an effective police force on the ground. In effect, that means that the rationale for treating detention as the rule and provisional release as exceptional disappears, and at that moment I would submit it's simply a question of considering the arguments of both parties and not considering that there's a substantial burden on the Defence which is very onerous for the Defence to discharge. It's simply a question of whether you are satisfied that the accused will appear for trial. And I would submit that even the Prosecution -- can they, hand on heart, say with all these conditions imposed, they genuinely fear that the accused will not appear for trial or will interfere with witnesses? I submit that they can't and that you can be satisfied, with the curfew or the house arrest, that the accused certainly will reappear. We also have an additional undertaking which General Alagic has signed with respect to his willingness to abide by any restrictions on his movement and not to interfere with any documents. And unless I can assist you any further, those would be my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We would appreciate to have this in writing too. It facilitates our deliberations. One question only remaining, just to be quite clear on this issue. It was submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor, quoting an affidavit, that the return from Croatia was not a voluntary one. Could you please address this question once more? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a question for Mr. Kubura, I believe. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel will start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, that was the first matter that I wished to deal with, which is whether or not he knew about the indictment when he was in Croatia. In his affidavit, he makes quite clear that when he was contacted while on an annual leave in Croatia, that he was told about the indictment. He didn't have a copy of the indictment at that stage, but he knew of the indictment issued by the Tribunal in general terms, and that is why he returned from Croatia to Sarajevo, in order to sort this matter out. He didn't bring his family back, because he didn't want his family to be there while this matter was to be dealt with, and he was going to make arrangements for his family to return later. The reason why, in the affidavit of Mr. Lusija, that it states - and I'm looking at the affidavit now, which is in enclosure 1 of our reply - that Mr. Kubura said that "You should have told me this straight away" is that he's referring to the order of the Supreme Court. He's referring to the order of the Supreme Court. He didn't know that the Supreme Court had issued an order for his extradition. This came as a surprise to him. And that's why in the affidavit you get the comment later on that he felt somewhat aggrieved by the situation, because he had said all along, "If there's ever an indictment, I would go to The Hague. There's no problem. I will surrender myself. So why did you therefore have to take this procedure of going through the national courts and getting an extradition order for my detention?" And that's the reason why he said, "Well, you should have told me about this straight away, because if I knew that, if I knew I was going to be arrested right now, as you're telling me, well, then I would have brought my family back." He was under the impression that there would be some time after the indictment was issued for him to make arrangements, to sort out matters with the Bosnian government, with his family, and then to be transferred to The Hague, and that is, we would submit, indicative of his state of mind at the time, that he did wish to surrender voluntarily. He did not think that there would be any need for an arrest of this kind. Your Honour, just a few further matters. The first, in relation to his arrest, we would submit that the Prosecution's arguments that it wasn't voluntary because he was already detained under this extradition order before he decided to hand himself over is really a matter of splitting hairs. It's very artificial. Mr. Kubura came back from Croatia because of the indictment, and he intended to surrender and he was arrested because he wanted to be transferred to The Hague. That was the whole purpose of this exercise. There's no other reason why he would have surrendered if it wasn't because of the indictment in The Hague. So that argument, we submit, has got no merit. I also wish to underline that it is significant that the Prosecutor has accepted that the government's guarantees are sufficient and that they are sufficient in practice as well. I think - and I might be wrong here - that this is probably the first case ever where the Prosecution has accepted guarantees from a government with regard to the release of an accused. I think that is very significant to bear in mind for this case. In addition, a number of smaller matters. The Prosecution has raised that it might make the case look weaker or sour relations between Croats and Muslims if these accused were released. We submit that those are considerations that form no part of such an application. In fact, in many jurisdictions, if the case is weak, that is a reason why the defendants should be released, because of the strength, or lack thereof, of evidence against the accused. Secondly, in respect of willingness to testify, that has been held already to not be a consideration either, that witnesses might now not be willing. It's a matter that can't be accurately determined anyway. It's a general statement. Thirdly, the trial date that was mentioned of April 2002, that's incorrect. There's no trial date been fixed in this matter yet. The matter is open. The parties are endeavouring, as is Mr. Kubura, to ensure that the trial starts as soon as possible. And the aim is to try and start it next year, but there's no fixed date yet. So if provisionally released, there would be, we say, a substantial time that they would be out of custody before the trial commences. Then on the point made by the Prosecutor that Mr. Kubura didn't cooperate fully when he came to the Tribunal for the Blaskic case, if the you consider that testimony, you will note that he answered many questions in respect of the matters in hand in that case, and others, about what was occurring. He was full and frank there, and fully cooperated both in travelling to The Hague and also answering questions and returning. And then finally, there was a question raised about his salary, whether he's still receiving a salary from the Bosnian government. If Your Honours look at our reply, it's quite clear that he's no longer receiving any income from the Bosnian government. As a result of the indictment, he no longer holds an official position in the Bosnian army, and that is the reason why there are financial difficulties being experienced now with his family, and it's because of those hardships that he has indicated if he was able to return, he could obtain employment and once again become the breadwinner of his family. Your Honours, those are my submissions. My final point would be that in the circumstances of Mr. Kubura returning from Croatia back to Bosnia as a result of this indictment, that it is a very unique situation for him to have done that, and it certainly provided opportunities at the time for him to abscond if he ever had that idea, but he came back. It's very unique. Once again, I cannot think of a situation where that has occurred in exactly the same way before. Those are our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, I would invite the Office of the Prosecutor, in a way of rebuttal, to address the question raised by the Trial Chamber. What is, from your point of view, the distinguishing factor, the distinguishing facts justifying a different treatment in the case of Madam Plavsic and the case we have to decide on today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I'm going to answer this particular question, I want to make a few additional observations. The Prosecution strongly opposes to introduce the case against Halilovic in these proceedings. The case against Halilovic, the accused Halilovic, is a very different one, not only with regard to cooperation but also with regard to other issues that are of relevance for the issue of granting provisional release. Secondly, the explanation that was given by Mr. Kubura's Defence with regard to the affidavit, it's not necessarily convincing. For me, it's still surprising that Mr. Kubura did not take his family with him home to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe you have made this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I will come to the distinguishing factors. I mean, there are a few distinguishing factors. One of them, of course, is the age of the accused in the other case and in this case. And there's also a distinguishing factor insofar as Mrs. Plavsic has cooperated with the Tribunal. That's very different from the situation to our accused. But therefore, before I come to an end, I want to request an additional guarantee. The Prosecution requests that if provisional release will be granted, that there will be no contact of the accused with each other. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to have a fair trial, you should have the possibility to address. Please, one sentence only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I apologise. This was a matter that I left out in my initial submission, that is, that there is also a declaration by Mr. Kubura, to be signed by him, indicating, as was specifically raised by Your Honours, that he will not try to gain access to any documents if provisionally released and that he will comply with any measure regarding restrictions in his movement within a town or area as has been proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comments from the side of Defence? I don't see any. Then we invite the accused, if they want to give a statement. And this is, of course, a statement of the accused applying Rule 84 bis correspondingly. That will say it's not a kind of witness statement but the right of the accused to address the Trial Chamber directly. Mr. Kubura, do you want to address the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KUBURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please rise and come to -- could you please come here and take the place where normally is the place of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED KUBURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to put forward certain elements with respect to my request for provisional release. What I have to say is the following: First of all, in viewing the entire area of the former Yugoslavia, starting with the Republic of Croatia via the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, we can quite certainly say and we agree that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina has had exemplary cooperation with the Tribunal so far, and an indication of this and proof of this is that there is not a single person or not the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina against whom an indictment has been raised by this Tribunal without that individual giving himself up voluntarily to the Tribunal or being held in custody, which is not the case with the other areas and territories of the former Yugoslavia. The representatives of the government in this case and on this occasion, Deputy Minister for the Interior and Deputy Justice Minister, amongst other things, in the presentation they made a moment ago stressed these elements and facts. Furthermore, they also emphasised that we gave ourselves up voluntarily to The Hague Tribunal. And I will speak in my own personal name. On that occasion, they, as the regular representatives of the government, stressed through their briefing that we surrendered voluntarily. In addition to saying that the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has had excellent cooperation with the Tribunal thus far and in addition to the report they tendered a moment ago, I see no reason for not believing those two individuals and their government, the government they represent. Otherwise, this would be undermining the government if we compare it to other governments that have not hitherto fulfilled their obligations towards this court and Tribunal. In concrete terms, when it comes to my own particular case and me personally, on the 2nd of August this year, I was at the seaside with my wife and three children. In the morning, at 10.05, I was called by my commander and asked to come to the headquarters to report to him there. Let me emphasise that I was holidaying by the sea in Croatia, which is another state. I had a passport, as did my wife and my children. On the basis of a telephone conversation which lasted 10 to 15 minutes, I was able to assess and size up the situation. But in view of the communication lines, I was not able to talk about that concrete case. So that is -- it was my personal assessment and appraisal of the situation. I decided to return immediately and to go back to Sarajevo, and I told my wife that she should stay where she was with the children and that I would let her know in due course and tell her whether I would come and fetch her or whether I would send somebody to fetch her. I reached Sarajevo at about 1620 hours. I had a change of clothing and went to my headquarters to report to my commander. I told him that I wished to be allowed to go to Den Haag to defend myself and prove my innocence. I called my relative up and told him to go and fetch my family by car, and that's what he did that afternoon and in the course of the night, and he accomplished that by the morning. I went to my apartment, took the basic essentials, and went to the Ministry of the Interior, which means that I never had any contact with the police nor was I detained or taken into custody, nor did I have handcuffs on me or anything of the kind. I think that it was between 1900 and 2000 hours when I entered the Ministry of the Interior and remained there until the following morning. On the following morning, I signed a statement in the Ministry of Justice, stating that I wished to be provided transport to The Hague. So that was then the 3rd of August. On that morning, my wife and children were also brought to the Justice Ministry, and I spent half an hour with them in a room in the Ministry. I said goodbye to them and started out for The Hague. Let me mention that in the meantime, while I have been here, my family was moved out of the apartment that we were living in. My family is now in another apartment. And actually, I don't know where they are living because I never went to that apartment. I know the street they live in and the number of the house and that they are in Sarajevo. My wife is unemployed. Now with respect to my testimony in the Blaskic trial. I was invited by the Prosecution -- I was not invited either by the Prosecution or the Defence. I was invited by the Trial Chamber, and at that time - and it was 1999 - I could have agreed to come to testify or not agreed at the invitation of the Trial Chamber. The fact that I acquiesced proves that I cooperated with the Tribunal at that time. I agreed to come, and I came and testified. Now, this act on my part demonstrated my willingness to cooperate with the Tribunal. Let me also mention that so far, I have never been convicted of any criminal offence nor have any proceedings been brought against me. Your Honours, I have been informed in detail with Article 65 of the rules and regulations, so that if I am provisionally released, I hereby state that I will abide by the provisions of Rule 65 in its entirety and that I will adhere to any decision you see fit to make, as well as the guarantees that have been provided by the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I wanted to say, Your Honours. If you have any questions, I shall be willing to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated at your place once again. We now turn to Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Would you please come.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me this opportunity to say a few words, and I will not take long. I should like to begin by saying that I cannot avoid being disappointed and hurt why I wasn't given an honourable legal summons to come to the Tribunal, even if it were in the form of an indictment. I was one of the few people who, with the Prosecution, at the end of 1996 and 1997, cooperated not only from -- not only regarding the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility but whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Should such a need arise again in the future, I will be ready to cooperate. I will make no further comments about that. I consider myself to be here on an absolutely voluntary basis. Secondly, I wish to defend my honour and my freedom, and I wish to struggle for my family. I have a wife who is unemployed and two children who are students. Both are on the first year of the university. My daughter is studying law; my son, economics. They need me at this stage of their studies. I would like them to be good students. And I wish to solemnly declare here that I will appear in court at each hearing. Secondly, I declare that I will not represent a threat, nor will I bear any kind of influence on victims and witnesses. I also declare that I will implement all other additional orders made by this Trial Chamber and respect all the guarantees given here by the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. We now turn to Mr. Alagic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ALAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank you for giving me the opportunity of saying a few words here before you. I should also like to take advantage of this opportunity to greet the representatives of the Prosecution and also the representatives of the government from the country from which I come, from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Having listened to the reasons put forward and the problems that might arise if I were to be provisionally released, I do not think they can be upheld. My name is Alagic, my father's name is Redzo, and my first name is Mehmed. I have always cooperated with the representatives of the investigators of the Tribunal and the Prosecution, not only by giving certain statement but also by assessing in the field towards the detection and discovery of certain things in certain regions, and mass graves. As somebody who has gone through the war, I have had the opportunity -- and I could have had the opportunity of perhaps leaving my own country. Mr. President, President of this Trial Chamber, the only country I know is the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is my country. It is now a Federation, and my place of residence is there in the municipality of Sanski Most. The address is Kljucka, number 42. I am somebody who has been demobilised, but I have not been pensioned off immediately after the war, which means that I do not have the possibility, nor would I access documents of any kind. That can only be done with people who have specific authority and permission to do so. At the time in the past, the time for which the members of the Prosecution have accused me of having committed certain crimes during that period of time, I think that this Trial Chamber and this Tribunal will be -- bring in the correct decision with respect to those crimes and whether I committed them or not. Despite the difficult times, I am somebody who by my conduct and behaviour always endeavoured within the frameworks of my competencies in terms of reference to solve the questions and problems which five or six years after the war have become a cornerstone and stumbling-block. I always value sincerity. People who have made statements are also my good friends. They are my colleagues, my fellow soldiers, who were -- who had undertaken various missions in those regions. So I was not somebody who could have committed anything of that kind. The case which is being tried before this Tribunal and the case that I have -- that legal proceedings have been undertaken against me is that I overstepped my authorisation with respect to the budget and the resources within the budget, and part of the testimony so far has showed that the damages amount to 1.250 German marks. And the Court, in the first instance, did not recognise the decisions about the rebalance of the budget during that period. I do not want to discuss the decisions. I think that they are still the subject of similar proceedings, whether the rebalance of the budget will be adopted or not, and the Ministers can bear this out. I considered, at the time, that by adopting a decision to rebalance the budget, that the decision had been made on the use of those funds and resources. As to some additional questions with regard to expert reports, the cantonal court, which is a court of the first instance, did not accept all these reasons, and I lodged an appeal to the Supreme Court of the Federation with respect to the Court's ruling. Neither at that time nor otherwise - although some people might have arrived at the wrong conclusion - not even then was any pressure exerted on potential witnesses at that time. I am by nature a man who would never even envisage exerting pressure on anybody. The truth must be shown to be the truth by the truth. Now, whether there was voluntary surrender or, as the Prosecution stated, that it was an arrest without coercion, the gentlemen from the government were also able to call me up on the phone. They could have called me to come to Sarajevo from Sanski Most without sending a car or a driver or anybody else to fetch me. I would have come of my own free will. Your Honours of the Trial Chamber, I should like to have come as a citizen of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina by plane. I should like to have come directly to The Hague and not to have been transferred from one base in Bosnia-Herzegovina by a military transport plane to The Hague here. I can also state that I have nothing to fear, nor any restraints, because it is truly an honour and privilege to stand here before this Tribunal and Trial Chamber and to have the truth presented here and proved, the truth and only the truth. In one of the cases that was tried by this Tribunal in The Hague, I was invited to come to The Hague, and I came. I spent several days in The Hague, and I think that I made a statement on that occasion. But the questions that were asked me on that occasion were not quite clear to me so that I was not able to give any relevant information in that regard. I stand at your disposal. I am willing to accept every decision and ruling that you might make, all the measures that you might prescribe, and regardless of everything else, I am ready and willing to come here to The Hague, to the Tribunal, to this Court. May I just say that the only thing that could prevent me would be my death, because I am a living being, a human being, and that too can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ALAGIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have any questions, I shall be happy to reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As you may have seen, we discussed the further proceedings, and we decided that the case is not ripe for a decision today. We have to discuss some issues in depth, and therefore we will finalise this day. Let's call it a day now and start again tomorrow, 3.00 in the afternoon. Are there any obstacles from the parties as regards this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not from the side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections, so we meet again tomorrow, 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 6.17 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of December, 2001, at 3.00 p.m.
